text: I think I'm gonna try to write something here once in a while. Not a TIL so much as a free associative writing exercise. This time it came out very long but I hope someone might find it interesting to read. So, sequences given by linear recurrence relations. Given a linear recurrence relation that determines each new element of the sequence as a linear combination of the previous N elements, we obviously get an N dimensional space of solutions. The recurrence can be thought of as a polynomial in the translation operator T, such that the solutions form the null space of this polynomial. Over the complex numbers, we can factor this polynomial into factors of the form (T-aI)^n and use that to find the solutions. It's easy to see that T-aI gives geometric sequences with a ratio of 1/a, and it turns out that (T-aI)^n allows multiplying the geometric sequence by an (n-1)th degree polynomial. We can find the solutions coming from distinct factors form a direct sum and that gives us enough dimensions for the full solution. I don't _necessarily_ recommend verifying all these facts right now if someone is following along. This whole argument admits a cleaner formulation for the continuous analogue, constant coefficient homogenous linear ODEs of degree N. So I'll include it for that case. This time the size of the solution space is given by existence and uniqueness, and the polynomial is in the differentiation operator. The solution space to D^n is well familiar as consisting of (n-1)th degree polynomials, and this time there's a lovely perspective using the operator P_a that multiplies functions pointwise by e^ax. Taking the derivative of e^(ax)f(x) we have one term where f simply gets differentiated, and another term that looks like the original times a. That is, DPₐ = PₐD + aPₐ, which gives PₐDPₐ^(-1) = D - aI. This automatically converts the solution space of D^n to a solution space of (D-aI)^n simply by applying the operator to it. The discrete analogue to the differentiation operator would be a difference operator like D = T - I, a polynomial in which would be the same thing as the polynomials in T we considered before, just translated by 1. But this time they are not similar, since T is injective. null(D^n) = null( (T-I)^n ) can still be seen to consist of polynomials (this is relatively simple but a little nice to think about), and we can still verify that the solutions to (T-aI)^n just need to be multiplied by a geometric sequence, but this time it's not nicely described by a similarity transformation, and there's an exception at a=0 because T is injective. Originally, I found this special behaviour at a=0 very offputting. Specifically because in the continuous case the symmetry was able to be described as a similarity transformation that had the effect of translating a polynomial in D, and now such a transformation could not exist even between distinct nonzero a's since it would translate a nonzero a to 0, even though all the other (T-aI) appear perfectly similar to before judging by their null spaces. So far, we didn't consider this detail, but for the description of the solutions as the null space of a polynomial in T to be fully correct, we need to assume the sequence is actually valued over Z, not just N, otherwise it's only the terms past the first N that can be expressed correctly as a linear combination. But let's run with that for a second, and consider sequences that only begin to satisfy the recurrence relation after some finite point. We might as well write the sequence as a formal power series in x, and our T from before was just multiplying by x, such that the linear recurrence is multiplying by a polynomial in x. Now, if our polynomial is divisible by x, that clearly does nothing to help it kill off a power series, so we might as well remove that factor. The nicest normalization is to let the constant coefficient be -1, so the coefficients of the powers of x are precisely the coefficients of the recurrence relation. Now, we see asking a power series f((x)) to eventually satisfy a recurrence relation is the same as asking for an equation q(x)f((x)) = p(x) for polynomials p,q. That is, f((x)) should be the Taylor series of a rational function. The recurrence relation limits the growth as to guarantee a positive radius of convergence, so we see that all our power series were exactly the Taylor series of rational functions that don't have a pole at 0. Fixing a recurrence relation and looking at its solutions amounts to fixing a denominator q(x). And now if p(x) is not relatively prime to q(x), the function might be expressible with a simpler denominator, describing how the sequence in fact lies in a smaller space of solutions to a simpler recurrence relation. The absolute bound on how large the sequence can grow then corresponds to the distance to the nearest pole of f(x). Which is the root of smallest absolute value in the simplest recurrence relation describing the sequence. Two such sequences will agree on all but a finite number of terms if the difference is a polynomial, that is, if they have the same proper fraction part. The proper fractions can then be seen to correspond to solutions that are determined by the recurrence relation precisely beginning at the (N+1)th element, leading us to an N dimensional space again. Taking out the singular part from each pole to get the partial fraction expansion, we get precisely the same breakdown of the solutions as we did by factoring the operators originally, but now thought of in terms of generating functions, and it's getting easier to distinguish now which properties are essential to each sequence, vs just describing the general solution space as a whole in general form. What essentially came from (T-aI)^n before is what we now describe as the term 1/(x-a)^n. Up to multiplying by a nonzero constant we can turn it into (a/(a-x))^n = 1/(1-(x/a))^n which precisely describes the symmetry that caused the solutions to (T-aI)^n to look the same for every n up to multiplying by an appropriate geometric sequence. And the singular behaviour at a=0 is inherently explained by this perspective, since the rational function can't have a pole at 0.

text: This is a funny story, but there is some real truth to it. Hilbert actually did not invent the abstract definition of Hilbert Spaces as we know them today (i.e. a Hilbert space is a complete inner-product space.) that was Von Neumann (who named them after Hilbert). Instead Hilbert generalized the notion of an inner-product space over functions with discrete eigenvalues (which had existed and been used in mathematics since at least the invention of Sturm-Liouville theory in the early 19th century), to a continuous spectrum. So, ironically, Hilbert was neither the first to invent a Hilbert Space nor was he the last to contribute to the theory. Instead he provided the critical connecting tissue that truly allowed the theory to generalize beyond the well-known examples.
